Hi Nic,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search and recovery for lab automation. I've built a system that finds deadlocks and searches for a way out of them.

I was reading about Agtonomy's multi-point turns. Finding the small change in available space that stops a manoeuvre from completing looks close to the search work I do.

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op. If the autonomy team has turning cases it wants reproduced, I could build a simulation search around the existing planner, reduce the failures to small test cases and work on an agreed fix.

Is there a turning or recovery issue waiting for that work? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if there is.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Nic,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Agtonomy's multi-point turns and got interested in the cases right at the edge of what the machine can complete, where a small change in available space means the same plan no longer works.

That's pretty close to what I spend a lot of my time on now: finding the conditions that make a plan fail and then searching for a way out. I've also been wanting to use more of that work on physical systems where getting the planning right actually changes what the machine can get done.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build simulated turning cases around those limits and test how the planner recovers as the available space changes, but if there’s another autonomy problem the team actually needs help with, I’d be happy to work on that instead.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on planning and simulation for lab automation. I've built a digital twin and a layout optimizer for reducing robot travel.

I was looking at Amperon's probabilistic wind and solar forecasts. One piece I could take on is the tooling for replaying historical forecasts against what actually happened, while keeping each run tied to the forecast available at that time.

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op. If there is manual work in that evaluation pipeline, I could automate a contained part of it and hand over a runner with tests and reproducible results.

Does your team have a backtesting task that needs an engineer? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if it does.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Kalpana,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Amperon's probabilistic wind and solar forecasts and got interested in how a backtest keeps track of successive forecast versions. A comparison only reflects the decision someone could have made if it uses the forecast they actually had at that moment, rather than a later revision.

That's close to the simulation work I do, where a replay needs to preserve what the system knew before each choice. I'd like to apply more of that work to energy forecasting, particularly the tooling that makes evaluations easier to reproduce and trust.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build a backtest workflow that aligns forecast issuance times with the later observations and checks that later revisions cannot enter earlier decisions, but I'd rather shape it around whichever forecast-data or evaluation problem would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Replanning as flexibility prices change
body:
Hi Archy,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading Axle's price-curve documentation and got interested in what happens when the price signal changes after part of the original battery schedule has already run. At that point you're not really optimizing from scratch anymore; you're replanning around the energy you've already used and what the user still needs.

That's close to the planning work I'm already doing, and lately I've been looking for ways to apply more of it to energy and other problems where better decisions have a real-world effect.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to compare replanning strategies as successive price curves arrive and see which ones still meet the user's energy needs, but I'd much rather work on whatever flexibility-planning problem would actually be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if there might be something worth working on, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Dylan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Bearing's schedule-recovery work and got interested in the decision to make up time before the next port. If the next delay is still uncertain, using more fuel now may not buy back as much useful time as the original recovery plan suggests.

A lot of my planning work is about finding a useful way forward after the assumptions behind a plan change. Shipping seems like an interesting place to apply that, because the choice has a direct consequence for both the remaining voyage and the fuel used.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. I could build a voyage-recovery backtest around agreed delay scenarios and compare when the time savings hold up, but I'd be happy to work on whichever planning or simulation problem would be most useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Recovery when orchard visibility changes
body:
Hi Ugur,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading Bonsai's explanation of distinguishing vegetation from obstacles in an orchard. The part that interested me was what happens when visibility gets worse halfway through a manoeuvre: a route that looked possible a moment ago may no longer give the machine enough information to continue.

That feels close to the failure and recovery work I do now, where the interesting part is often how a small change removes the options a planner was relying on. I'd like to apply more of that work to agricultural machines dealing with conditions outside a controlled lab.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build simulated cases where visibility changes, compare the recovery choices and keep the difficult cases as repeatable tests, though I'd rather shape it around an autonomy problem the team actually needs help with.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Recovering a hospital delivery plan
body:
Hi Vivian,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Moxi's hospital deliveries and got interested in what happens to the rest of a delivery plan when one route becomes temporarily unavailable. Waiting may preserve the original order, but doing another delivery first could avoid holding up work that is still possible.

That's close to the recovery planning I work on in biotech automation, where one blocked step can affect several later tasks. I've been wanting to apply more of that work to physical systems that take practical work off people's hands.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that kind of planning. One idea would be to compare waiting and reordering in an offline delivery simulation, but I'd rather work on whichever recovery problem would actually be useful to the Moxi team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Nicolas,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search and recovery for lab automation. I've built a system that finds deadlocks and searches for a way out of them.

With Silvanet, I'd like to help on the software between a sensor reading and a fire alert. If delayed or missing messages are difficult to reproduce in your backend tests, I could build a replay tool that injects those gaps and records when the alert changes.

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op, and could own that through to runnable tests in your existing setup.

Does your team have any message-handling cases waiting for that kind of coverage? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if so.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Nicolas,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Silvanet's combination of sensors and a wireless network for early fire detection. It got me thinking about the path from a useful observation to an alert: a delayed message matters differently depending on whether it contains the first sign of a change or repeats something already known.

That's close to the failure-sequence work I do in automation, where the order and timing of otherwise ordinary events can change the outcome. I'd like to use more of that work on environmental systems where time to act is part of what makes the software useful.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build repeatable sensor-message sequences with controlled delays and test the resulting alert timing, but I'd rather work on whichever part of the message or alert workflow your team needs help with.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Interrupted writes and Icechunk recovery
body:
Hi Brian,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Icechunk's transaction model and the fault-injection work in the Icechunk 2 release. What caught my attention was the sequence of events around an interrupted write, particularly when other writes are happening at the same time and each individual operation looks reasonable.

That's close to the search work I already do: finding sequences of valid actions that leave an automated system in a state it can't cleanly recover from. I'd like to apply more of that work to scientific software, where people need to trust the state a long computation leaves behind.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to extend the existing fault-injection work with a set of interrupted or overlapping write cases and reduce failures to reproducible tests, but I'd rather start with whichever storage or recovery problem would actually help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Recovering a field plan after a blocked route
body:
Hi Michael,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about TerraMax operating under canopy and in difficult field conditions. What caught my attention was how a blocked route changes the rest of a field plan: the machine may still be able to do most of the work, but not in the order it originally intended.

That's close to the recovery planning I do now, where I search for a useful continuation after one action becomes impossible. I'd like to apply more of that work to agricultural systems operating in less predictable conditions than a lab.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build blocked-route cases in simulation and compare how the planner reaches the remaining work, but I'd rather shape it around whichever autonomy or recovery problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Battery dispatch across successive charging peaks
body:
Hi Sith,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Electric Era combining grid power and battery storage for charging. What interested me was the choice to use stored energy during one demand peak when another could arrive before the battery has recovered. The best response to the first peak may depend on what it leaves possible afterward.

That connects to the planning work I already do, where an action can solve the immediate problem while removing later options. I'd like to apply more of that work to energy systems, especially where the plan has to meet real demand with finite physical resources.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build successive-demand scenarios and compare battery dispatch choices under the same site constraints, but I'd rather shape it around whichever charging-software or evaluation problem would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Recovering a charging schedule after reconnection
body:
Hi Mauro,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Enode connecting and controlling energy devices and got interested in what happens when a charger reconnects after missing part of a schedule. The original plan may still be available, but the energy already delivered and the time remaining could now call for a different one.

That feels close to the recovery work I do in automation, where continuing means first accounting for the state the system actually reached. I've been wanting to apply more of that work to energy systems that have to deal with real devices and imperfect communication.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to simulate missed commands and reconnection, then compare how a charging schedule recovers, but I'd rather shape it around whichever device-control or integration problem would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: When a process recommendation reaches a constraint
body:
Hi Todd,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Fero's process simulation and setpoint recommendations and got interested in the conditions just beyond a promising recommendation. A setting that looks useful at the current operating point might behave differently when another input moves, even if the change seems small on its own.

That connects to how I use simulation and search in automation, looking for the conditions that make a plan stop working. I'd like to apply more of that work to industrial tools where understanding the limits of a recommendation is part of making it useful.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build parameter sweeps around an agreed process model and identify the combinations that cross its operating constraints, but I'd rather start with whichever simulation or evaluation problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Daniel,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search and recovery for lab automation. I've built a system that finds deadlocks and searches for a way out of them.

I was looking at the GR-100's collision-free motion planning. The part that overlaps with my work is what happens after an approach cannot finish: finding a way to continue without repeatedly attempting the same blocked move.

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op. If you have failed approaches that are difficult to reproduce, I could turn them into simulation tests and work through an agreed recovery change, leaving the code and regression cases with your team.

Is anything like that on the robotics backlog? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if so.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Recovering after a harvesting approach is blocked
body:
Hi Daniel,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about the GR-100's collision-free motion planning and got interested in what happens when an approach to one tomato becomes unavailable. Trying another approach may preserve the original order, while moving to another tomato first could open a better continuation.

That's close to what I do now: finding a useful sequence after the action a system intended to take is no longer possible. I'd like to apply more of that planning work to agricultural robots dealing with physical spaces that are difficult to predict exactly.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build blocked-approach cases in simulation and compare recovery choices, including testing an agreed planner change, but I'd rather shape it around whichever harvesting or motion-planning problem would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Which pick leaves the best next choice?
body:
Hi Rebecca,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Glacier's sorting robots and got interested in the choice between a good pick now and a better sequence of picks just behind it. With material moving past the robot, the value of a choice depends partly on what it leaves time to recover next.

That connects quite naturally to the search and planning work I do in automation. I've also been looking for ways to apply it where the decisions have a tangible result, and recovering more useful material from a waste stream is an appealing version of that.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build and compare pick-selection logic on recorded or simulated streams, looking at what each strategy recovers under the same conditions, though I'd rather start with the planning problem the team actually needs help with.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on planning and simulation for lab automation. I've built a digital twin and a layout optimizer for reducing robot travel.

Gridraven's span-level weather modelling caught my attention. I could help automate tests that vary the weather inputs and show which span causes the line's rating to change, with each result tied back to the exact inputs.

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op. If your engineers still run parts of that analysis manually, I could build it around the existing model and the checks they specify, then leave you with a repeatable test runner.

Is there a sensitivity-testing task on the team's backlog? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if so.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Weather uncertainty at the limiting span
body:
Hi Henri,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Gridraven's local weather modelling for line ratings. The part that interested me was how a change at one span could change the useful capacity of the whole line, even when the weather estimates elsewhere barely move.

My simulation work often involves finding the small change that makes a constraint become the limiting one. I'd like to use more of that work on energy systems, where understanding that boundary can affect how existing infrastructure is used.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build weather-input sensitivity tests around an agreed rating model and identify which spans drive changes in the result, but I'd rather work on whichever modelling or evaluation problem would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Missing observations near an operating threshold
body:
Hi Bryce,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about CoastAware's local measurements and forecasts for marine operations. It got me thinking about gaps in observations near an operating limit: a gap during steady weather may change very little, while the same gap as conditions turn could change whether an operation looks possible.

That distinction is close to the simulation work I do, where I try to find which changes actually alter the decision a system can make. I've been looking for ways to use more of that work on environmental data that people rely on in the physical world.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around this. One idea would be to replay weather windows with selected observations withheld and see which gaps change an agreed operating-threshold decision, but I'd rather start with whatever forecast-evaluation problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Replanning a survey as the energy budget changes
body:
Hi Ari,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about DataXplorer's solar-powered surveys and got interested in what happens when the available energy changes partway through a mission. The original route may no longer be the most useful one, but returning early can also leave a very different pattern of missing survey coverage.

That's close to the constrained planning I do in automation, where recovery means deciding which useful work is still possible from the current state. I'd like to apply more of that work to environmental observation with machines operating outside a controlled setting.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to compare survey-plan adaptations in simulation under changing energy and weather assumptions, but I'd rather start with whichever mission-planning question would actually be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

subject: Material-recognition changes that matter for sorting
body:
Hi Matthew,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Recycleye's vision and robotic sorting work and got interested in the ambiguous material detections. A model change might improve its overall result while making a particular material mix harder to distinguish, which seems especially worth understanding when the classifications guide physical sorting.

I've also worked on evaluating a distilled robot policy against its larger teacher, so checking what a model change preserves is something I've spent time on. I'd like to use more of that work on practical systems such as recycling, where the errors have a visible consequence.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build a repeatable evaluation around agreed labelled examples and compare where material classifications change between model versions, but I'd rather shape it around whichever ML-evaluation problem would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build delayed-trip cases and compare schedule repairs against the same break and service constraints, keeping the difficult cases reproducible, but I'd rather work on whichever algorithms problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Celia,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on planning and simulation for lab automation. I've built a digital twin and a layout optimizer for reducing robot travel.

I was looking at the AIS data behind Searoutes' routing and emissions calculations. A gap in a vessel's track seems like a useful regression case: changing the reconstructed route can also change the emissions estimate.

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op. If your team has track-gap cases that still need manual checking, I could turn them into automated tests with reproducible inputs and a clear record of which results changed.

Is that a piece of the data-quality backlog someone could take on? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if it is.

Best,
Andrew

subject: AIS gaps that change the reconstructed route
body:
Hi Celia,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about how Searoutes combines routing and cleaned AIS data for emissions calculations. I got interested in gaps where more than one route could connect the visible positions, because choosing between them could change the distance and the emissions estimate without changing the observations on either side.

That feels close to the simulation and search work I do, where incomplete information can leave several plausible explanations. I'd like to apply more of it to environmental calculations, especially where understanding the uncertainty helps someone use the result sensibly.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to replay known routes with selected AIS sections removed and build repeatable cases where reconstruction changes the estimate, but I'd rather shape it around whichever routing or data-evaluation problem would be useful to your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Sepehr,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about AutoCode and got interested in the inspection results that sit near a model's confidence boundary. Sending every uncertain case for review may catch more errors, but it also matters whether the extra review is spent on cases that change the final inspection record.

I've also worked on evaluating a distilled robot policy against its larger teacher, which made me interested in understanding the errors hidden by an overall score. I'd like to apply more of that evaluation work to practical infrastructure such as sewer inspection.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to compare review-selection rules on an agreed labelled inspection set, looking at important missed findings as well as review volume, but I'd rather shape it around whichever model or workflow evaluation would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,

subject: How one delayed pickup changes the rest of a route
body:
Hi Diogo,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Spare's real-time routing for microtransit and paratransit and got interested in the recovery after a delayed pickup. Reordering the next few stops might improve the vehicle's schedule while moving the delay onto someone who was already expecting a particular pickup time.

That feels close to the planning work I do, where recovering a sequence means looking beyond the first task that went wrong. I'd like to use more of that work on transport systems where the tradeoffs affect people directly.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to replay delayed-pickup scenarios and compare the knock-on passenger delays and schedule changes from different repairs, but I'd rather shape it around whichever routing-evaluation problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Ask,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Spoor's bird tracking around wind farms and got interested in the short gaps where a bird disappears from view. Depending on what happened during that gap, the same visible track could suggest quite different accounts of how close it came to a turbine.

My current work involves searching for small changes that remove a recovery option. I'd like to use more of that simulation work on environmental problems, and testing what can actually be inferred from an incomplete track felt like a useful connection.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to replay tracks with controlled visibility gaps and build repeatable cases where the inferred encounter changes, but I'd rather shape it around a tracking-evaluation question the team already needs answered.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Is there a prediction-feed testing task on your team's backlog? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if there is.

Best,
Andrew

subject: When a missing vehicle update removes an ETA
body:
Hi Zubin,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading Swiftly's ETA Completeness Benchmark and liked the distinction between an accurate prediction and a prediction that actually reaches the rider. It got me thinking about missing vehicle updates: some gaps may leave an ETA usable, while others could make the prediction disappear just when someone needs it.

That connects to the failure-sequence work I do in automation, where the timing of missing information can matter more than the amount missing. I'd like to use more of that work on systems whose reliability changes an everyday decision for someone using them.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to replay vehicle-update traces with controlled gaps and evaluate where ETA completeness changes, but I'd rather work on whichever prediction-feed or data-platform problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: When missing readings change event detection
body:
Hi Boaz,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about TaKaDu's detection of water-network events and got interested in the difference between a missing reading during normal operation and one as a leak or pressure event is developing. The size of the data gap alone doesn't seem to tell you how much useful warning it removes.

That connects to the simulation work I do, where I try to find which changes actually affect what a system can detect or recover from. I've been looking for ways to apply more of that work to practical infrastructure, particularly when earlier information helps people act.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to replay agreed network traces with missing or delayed readings and identify the cases where detection changes, but I'd rather shape it around whichever event-evaluation problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Choosing which rocks to reach first
body:
Hi Brent,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about TerraClear's rock maps and how they guide field travel. What interested me was the choice of which rocks to prioritize when there isn't time to cover the whole field: the shortest route and the route that removes the most troublesome rocks may be quite different.

I've worked on layout and planning problems where reducing travel only helps if the useful work still gets done. I'd like to apply more of that optimization work to agricultural systems, where the result is something an operator can actually use in the field.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to compare routes and removal priorities within an agreed operating window, using a small simulation to make the tradeoffs visible, but I'd be happy to shape the work around whichever planning question matters most to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: When uncertainty changes treatment priorities
body:
Hi Chris,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about the Pyrologix modelling behind Vibrant Planet's treatment planning. The question that caught my attention was when uncertainty in the model actually changes which area gets treated first, rather than just moving the risk estimates a little.

That's close to the simulation and search work I do, where I'm interested in the conditions that change a decision. I've been looking for ways to apply more of it to environmental problems, especially where a model helps decide what practical work gets done.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build a sensitivity evaluation around an agreed model and identify which assumptions change the treatment ranking, but I'd rather work on whichever modelling question would actually be useful to your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op. I could build those scenarios around existing charging logic and leave the team with reproducible inputs and regression checks.

Do you have departure-change cases waiting to be automated? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if so.

Andrew

subject: Earlier departures under a local grid constraint
body:
Hi Owen,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about DISCO coordinating charging around distribution-grid constraints and got interested in an earlier departure request after charging has been allocated. The driver's new target may still be achievable, but only by changing other vehicles' schedules; in some cases there may simply be no feasible repair.

That's close to the recovery planning I do now, where part of the work is separating a difficult plan from one the current constraints make impossible. I've been looking for ways to apply more of that work to energy systems with practical needs on both sides of the schedule.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build departure-change cases and compare repairs under agreed local grid limits, but I'd rather work on whichever charging-planning or evaluation problem would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build an evaluation around an agreed formulation problem and compare selection strategies under its real constraints, but I'd rather work on whichever experiment-planning question would actually help the team.

subject: Turnaround plans with delayed event updates
body:
Hi Dmitry,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Assaia's turnaround monitoring and got interested in events that happen before the system learns about them. If a completion update arrives late, the next estimate may briefly be based on a task that is already finished, and that could matter differently depending on what follows it.

That's close to the planning work I do in automation, where the useful plan depends on both the physical state and what the system currently knows. I'd like to apply more of that work to operations with real timing and coordination constraints.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to replay turnaround traces with delayed or missing updates and compare the effect on estimated completion times, but I'd rather start with whichever event or planning problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Alex,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Atmo's forecasts for operational users and got interested in heavy-rain events where a small timing error matters more than a similar error on an ordinary day. A forecast can be fairly close overall and still provide too little lead time before an important threshold is reached.

The simulation work I do often comes down to finding which errors change what a system can do next. I'd like to apply more of that evaluation work to environmental problems, where the timing of a prediction can make a practical difference.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build an evaluation around historical rain events and an agreed threshold, comparing the lead time available from successive forecasts, but I'd rather shape it around whichever forecasting question would be most useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Repairing a robot path after a part moves
body:
Hi Daryl,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Augmentus generating robot motion from 3D scans and got interested in a small change to a part's pose after a path has been planned. Sometimes adjusting a short section may be enough; in other cases, that local repair could leave the robot with no workable continuation.

That distinction is close to the planning and recovery work I already do. I've been wanting to apply more of it to physical automation, where the useful answer is whether the machine can still finish the job from the state it's actually in.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build offline cases around changed part poses and compare local path repair with replanning, keeping the difficult cases as repeatable tests, but I'd rather work on whichever planning problem would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Recovering dispatch when assets drop out together
body:
Hi Clement,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Beebop's virtual power plant orchestration and got interested in what happens when several assets become unavailable for the same reason. A dispatch plan with enough room for individual dropouts could behave quite differently when those losses happen together.

That's close to the recovery planning I do now, where the useful question is what remains possible after several assumptions change at once. I've been looking for ways to apply more of that work to energy systems with real commitments to meet.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build correlated-dropout scenarios and compare how a dispatch plan recovers under agreed constraints, but I'd rather work on whichever orchestration or modelling question would actually help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Replanning depot charging after an earlier departure
body:
Hi Roby,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Bia's fleet charging optimization and got interested in a vehicle needing to leave earlier after the depot's charging plan has already started. Giving that vehicle more power may solve its problem while changing whether the others will be ready on time.

That connects to the constrained planning I do in automation, where recovering one task can affect the rest of the schedule. I'd like to apply more of that work to electric fleets, where the plan has to work for the vehicles people actually need to use.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build a small depot simulation and compare recovery choices under the same power limit, looking at which departures remain achievable, but I'd rather shape it around a charging-planning problem that would be useful to your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Distinguishing forest change from uncertainty
body:
Hi Alessandro,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Chloris's biomass and change measurements and got interested in how uncertainty carries between observations. Two estimates can each look reasonable while the difference between them is still difficult to interpret as growth or loss.

That feels close to the model-evaluation side of my simulation work: understanding when uncertainty changes the conclusion, rather than just the number reported. I've been looking for ways to apply more of that work to environmental measurements people use to decide what to do.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build an evaluation around a reference set and test when uncertainty changes the inferred direction or size of biomass change, but I'd rather work on whichever change-detection question would be useful to the science team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Continuing layout after a positioning interruption
body:
Hi Tom,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Civ's use of RTK positioning for construction layout and got interested in what happens when a good position estimate briefly becomes unavailable. Waiting in place, moving to another part of the job and revisiting later seem like choices whose value depends on what is still left to mark.

That connects to the recovery planning I do now, where the question is how to continue useful work after one part of the original plan stops being possible. I'd like to do more of it on machines working in the physical world.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build offline positioning-interruption cases and compare waiting, revisiting and replanning against agreed accuracy requirements, but I'd be happy to work on whichever navigation or recovery problem is actually useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Recovering an interrupted simulation run
body:
Hi Matthew,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about running scientific simulations with Coiled and got interested in what happens when a large run is interrupted after some of the work has finished. Restarting the computation is one thing; knowing which results are complete and which still need to be produced is another.

I run simulations as part of my planning work, so this feels close to the tools I'd like to spend more time building. Making a long experiment easier to resume and trust would be a useful way to apply the recovery side of what I do.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build a simulation example with controlled interruptions and test that the final outputs contain everything expected without duplicates, but I'd rather work on whichever part of the scientific-computing workflow would actually help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Finding the smallest scene change that breaks recovery
body:
Hi Apurva,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Falcon and got interested in using simulation to work backwards from a successful recovery. If a robot can get out of a difficult situation, what is the smallest change to the scene that makes the same recovery stop working? That seems like a useful way to find cases a broad scenario sweep might miss.

It's close to the search work I do now, where I look for the conditions that make a plan fail and then try to find a way out. I'd like to do more of that work with simulation tools that help engineers understand how a physical system behaves.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build that search around an agreed Falcon scene and reduce the resulting failures to reproducible cases, but I'd rather shape it around whichever scenario-generation or evaluation problem would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Felix,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on planning and simulation for lab automation. I've built a digital twin and a layout optimizer for reducing robot travel.

I was reading about envelio's GPU power-flow work. One piece I could take on is generating load and generation combinations near the network's operating limits, with each result reduced to an input case the team can rerun.

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op. Working within limits your engineers define, I could build the scenario search and automated checks around an existing solver interface, then leave the tests in your repository.

Does the solver team have a set of boundary cases it wants automated? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if so.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Small network changes near a constraint
body:
Hi Felix,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about envelio's GPU-based power-flow calculation and got interested in what the faster calculations make possible for testing. Rather than only running more typical cases, there seems to be room to search around the cases where a small network change alters which constraint is limiting.

That's close to how I use simulation in my current work: searching for the boundary where a plan stops working, then understanding what caused it. I'd like to apply more of that work to energy tools that engineers use to assess real networks.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build a search over agreed network scenarios and keep the boundary cases as reproducible solver tests, but I'd rather work on whichever algorithm or evaluation problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: When several departure times change together
body:
Hi Steve,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about ev.energy's charging and flexibility modelling and got interested in changes that affect several drivers at once. A charging plan might cope well with one person leaving early, but several people making the same change could leave a very different set of options.

That's close to the planning work I do now, where a few changed constraints can make a previously workable plan impossible. I've been looking for ways to apply more of that work to energy, especially where better scheduling helps without asking people to change what they need from the system.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. I could build simulated departure changes and compare how the charging plan recovers, turning the difficult cases into repeatable tests, but I'd rather work on whichever flexibility-modelling question would actually be useful to your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Planning around the next reload
body:
Hi Bryce,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Flash Forest's drone planting and got interested in how a route changes when you account for the next battery change or seed-pod reload. Finishing the nearest patch first might look efficient locally while leaving a longer return trip or a less useful starting point for the next flight.

That connects to the layout and planning work I do in automation, where travel and the order of tasks affect how much work a system can finish. I'd like to use more of that work on environmental projects with a physical result, which is what drew me to the planting operation.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around the planning. One idea would be to build a route-and-reload simulation and compare coverage under the same battery and planting constraints, but I'd much rather start with whatever operational planning problem would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Finding the event behind a robot failure
body:
Hi Adrian,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Foxglove's work on searching and analysing robot data. What interested me was the difference between finding the loudest alarm and finding the earlier event that explains why recovery became difficult. Those could be quite far apart in a long recording.

I spend a lot of my time searching for failure and recovery sequences in automated systems, so that distinction feels familiar. I'd like to do more work on tools that help an engineer understand one of those sequences without having to reconstruct everything by hand.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build a set of robot-log cases with agreed explanations and evaluate whether the search brings up the relevant events, but I'd rather work on whichever part of investigating robot failures would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: What the rest of a fleet does when one robot pauses
body:
Hi Hernan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about InOrbit coordinating intralogistics work across robots and business systems. I got interested in the moment one robot has to pause: leaving its task where it is might be sensible, but reassigning it could change the queues and dependencies for several other robots.

That's close to the recovery planning I do in automation, where getting one component moving again isn't always the same as recovering a useful plan for the whole system. I'd like to do more of that work on software coordinating real machines.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to simulate a paused task and compare waiting with reassignment, tracking what happens to the remaining work, but I'd rather shape it around whichever orchestration or recovery problem would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: When another simulation changes the design choice
body:
Hi Pierre,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Neural Concept's engineering models and got interested in two designs that receive very similar predictions. The useful question seems to be whether another full simulation would change which design you'd choose, rather than whether it would simply make one prediction more precise.

That connects to the simulation and search work I already do, where I try to spend computation on the cases that could change the next decision. I'd like to apply more of that work to design tools with a direct connection to physical engineering.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to compare predicted and simulated rankings on an agreed design set and evaluate which extra solver runs are most informative, but I'd rather work on whichever model-validation or design-search question would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Afshin,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about QuantStack's work on Jupyter applications, including JupyterLite, and got interested in taking a scientific computation into the browser. If the result changes between environments, reducing that difference to a small example seems useful both for the person running the experiment and the people maintaining the tools.

I use simulation for my planning work, so reliable scientific tooling is something I'd like to spend more time contributing to. The search for a small reproducible failure also feels close to what I do with larger automated systems.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to work through a browser-versus-native numerical issue and turn the reduced example into a regression test, but I'd rather start with whichever scientific-software problem would actually help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Logan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Rugged's construction layout work and got interested in what happens when part of the floor becomes temporarily unavailable after marking has started. The robot still has useful work it could do, but changing the order may affect how it returns to the unfinished area later.

That's close to what I work on in automation: recovering a useful sequence after one action becomes impossible, while keeping track of what has already happened. I'd like to apply more of that work to physical systems operating around people and changing spaces.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to compare layout sequences around temporary obstructions in simulation and see which finish the remaining work with less revisiting, but I'd rather shape it around a planning problem that would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

old.queue_subject: Solar layouts with uncertain roof geometry
old.queue_body:
Hi Jason,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

Building a layout optimizer has made me interested in when a small measurement error changes whether a plan fits at all. With Scanifly's remote solar design, I'd be curious which roof measurements matter most to the final panel layout when they're slightly wrong.

I could take ownership of a small sensitivity test around an agreed set of roofs, finding where a layout stops fitting as the geometry changes. Would that be useful as a contract project alongside my current work, or is there another layout question the team would rather have someone investigate?

Happy to send my resume over.

Best,
Andrew

subject: When a small geometry change alters a solar layout
body:
Hi John,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Scanifly's 3D design tools and got interested in layouts close to a roof edge or obstruction. A small change in the measured geometry might barely affect most of the design while changing whether one part of the layout still fits.

I've been working with simulation and layout optimization in automation, so the connection between a model and what can physically fit caught my attention. I'd like to apply more of that work to energy projects where the output is used to build something real.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build geometry-sensitivity tests on an agreed set of roofs and identify the changes that affect a layout's feasibility, but I'd rather shape it around a design-algorithm problem your team actually needs help with.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Resuming a simulation workflow after a failed stage
body:
Hi Mariano,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about SimScale's Workflows execution system and got interested in what happens when a later stage fails after earlier work has completed. The interesting recovery question is which outputs are still valid to reuse and which dependencies really need to run again.

That's close to the failure and recovery work I do in automation, where a restart has to account for the state the system has already reached. I'd like to use more of that work on scientific software, particularly where a small improvement can save someone from repeating a long computation.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build reproducible interruption cases around an agreed workflow and compare how it resumes, but I'd rather shape it around whichever recovery or simulation-infrastructure problem would actually help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on planning and simulation for lab automation. I've built a digital twin and a layout optimizer for reducing robot travel.

Timefold's constraint solving is close to the work I want to do more of. One useful piece I could own is testing what happens to a published schedule after a resource becomes unavailable, including how many unaffected assignments move.

I'm looking for a small paid contract outside my co-op. I could add those disruption cases to an existing benchmark and turn constraint violations or unexpected changes into small, reproducible tests.

Is there a schedule-repair testing task on the solver team's backlog? Happy to talk for 15 minutes if there is.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Repairing a schedule without changing everything
body:
Hi Geoffrey,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was looking through Timefold's planning work and got interested in what happens after a schedule is already in use. Once one assignment becomes impossible, finding another feasible schedule is only part of the problem; it also matters how much of everyone else's plan has to move.

That's close to the recovery work I do in automation, where I search for a way to continue from the state the system is already in. I'd like to do more of that kind of planning work on software people use to run real operations.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to add disruption cases to a scheduling example and compare repairs by feasibility and how much they change, but I'd much rather shape it around a solver or planning problem the team would find useful.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Design choices as the operating load changes
body:
Hi Marco,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about ToffeeX's physics-driven design work and got interested in designs that are close at one operating point but behave differently as the load changes. A small change in the load could reverse which design you'd choose even if the performance estimates only move a little.

That connects to the simulation and optimization work I already do, where I try to understand which assumptions change the preferred plan. I'd like to spend more time on that kind of computational work when it feeds into something that will actually be built.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build a comparison around an agreed set of designs and loads, showing where the preferred design changes, but I'd rather shape it around a design-evaluation problem that would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: When forest observations disagree
body:
Hi Jonathan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Treefera's use of satellite and ground evidence and got interested in the cases where two observations suggest different things happened in the same area. The useful next step seems to depend on what would distinguish those explanations, rather than simply collecting another observation of the same kind.

That connects to the search side of my work, where I try to find which next action actually changes what we know or can do. I've been looking for ways to use more of that work on environmental data that supports real decisions.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build a reproducible set of evidence disagreements and compare which additional observations resolve them against agreed reference cases, but I'd rather start with whichever evidence-evaluation problem would help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Choosing experiments before a batch has finished
body:
Hi Katie,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Uncountable's experimental R&D workflows and got interested in the point where some results from a batch are available but others are still running. Waiting gives a more complete picture, but it can also leave the next round of useful experiments on hold.

That connects to the planning work I do in biotech automation, where tasks finish at different times and the next choice depends on what is known so far. I'd like to apply more of that work to software that helps researchers decide what to do next.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to replay an agreed experiment history and compare waiting with selecting the next tests from partial results, but I'd rather start with whichever experimental-workflow problem would actually be useful to your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

subject: Choosing what to test after an unexpected result
body:
Hi Aaike,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about VSPARTICLE's experimental datasets and automated material discovery. The part that interested me was what happens after a result disagrees with the current model: repeating a nearby experiment could clarify what went wrong, while trying something elsewhere could move the search forward faster.

That feels close to the search and planning work I do in biotech automation, where the next action depends on what the previous one revealed. I'd like to spend more time on computational work that helps decide which physical experiment is worth doing next.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to compare experiment-selection strategies on an existing dataset under the same testing budget, using the unexpected results as the starting cases, but I'd rather shape it around whichever evaluation would be useful to your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew
